conversation.content:
Hello there, I’m Dr. Miller, a clinician who specializes in the emotional well-being of new mothers. Today I’ll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually called the EPDS—to get a quick picture of how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. It’s simply 10 questions about the past seven days; your answers are confidential and will help me understand what support would be most helpful for you right now. We’ll take it one question at a time, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you. Ready to begin?

Over the past week, when you were able to laugh and see the funny side of things, how did that feel for you?

I’ve still laughed a little—like when my sister sent those silly memes—but it feels kind of forced. Most of the time the humor just doesn’t land the way it used to; it’s like I’m pretending to enjoy it more than I really do.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I guess I’d say “not quite so much now.” I still chuckle here and there, but it feels kind of flat—like I’m going through the motions rather than really feeling it.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but now it all feels like another chore. I’ll plan something and then wish I hadn’t bothered, because I don’t expect to enjoy it much when it happens.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that. If the baby’s fussy or won’t settle, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong—like I’m not a good-enough mom. I keep replaying what I did or didn’t do, even when people tell me it’s normal infant stuff.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Most days. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly worry her breathing sounds off, or I’ll lie down and picture her crib sheets bunching up around her face. There’s no real reason—it’s just this loop I can’t shut off. Sometimes I can talk myself down, but it pops right back up.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A few times this week—like last night when I was trying to sleep—my heart started racing and I felt shaky, convinced something awful was about to happen even though nothing was wrong. It passed after a few minutes, but it left me on edge the rest of the night.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes. Most of the time it feels like I’m barely treading water—laundry, bottles, trying to sleep, worrying about every little thing. I’ll be in the middle of something simple like changing her and suddenly feel completely swamped, like I can’t catch up or handle even one more task.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I lie down exhausted, but my head keeps spinning with all the “what-ifs” about the baby, and then I feel sad and guilty for feeling this way. It takes me over an hour to fall asleep most nights, and when I do wake up for her feeding, I can’t drift back off because the same thoughts start racing again.
I have felt sad or miserable

That’s pretty much how I feel most days. It’s not every single minute, but it’s like there’s this heavy cloud that settles over me—everything feels gray and I can’t shake the sadness, even when I’m doing things that are supposed to be nice.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… I’ve ended up in tears twice this week. Once was after a phone call when my mom asked how I was doing—I said “fine,” but as soon as I hung up I just started bawling. Another time the baby wouldn’t stop fussing and I felt like I was failing her; I put her in the crib for a minute, went to the bathroom, and cried over the sink so she wouldn’t hear.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

A couple of times, yeah. Nothing planned—just a quick, scary flash of “what if I weren’t here” when everything feels too heavy. It startles me and I push it away, but the fact that it popped in at all frightens me.

You've shared how the joy of new motherhood feels overshadowed by a constant heaviness: laughter is flat, simple pleasures now seem like chores, and waves of worry about your baby's safety and your own worth crash over you day and night. You described feeling swamped by everyday tasks, lying awake with racing thoughts, and moments of unexpected tears or even brief, frightening flashes of wondering if you and your baby might be better off without you. These feelings are understandably frightening, and I appreciate your openness in talking about them.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports complete loss of anticipatory pleasure, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient affirms frequent self-blame and describes persistent rumination about her perceived failures as a mother, matching "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes intrusive, persistent worries occurring "most days" with difficulty controlling the thoughts, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes discrete panic-like episodes (racing heart, dread, no trigger) occurring multiple times within the week, aligning with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling "barely treading water" and "completely swamped" most of the time, matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly sleep disruption linked to distressing thoughts and guilt, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent sadness "most days" and a pervasive "heavy cloud," aligning with "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes two distinct crying episodes this week triggered by emotional overwhelm, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports intrusive self-harm thoughts occurring "a couple of times," matching "Sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS items map to DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset: depressed mood most days (Q8 score 3), markedly diminished interest (Q2 score 3), insomnia (Q7 score 3), fatigue and feelings of worthlessness or excessive guilt (Q3 score 3), psychomotor agitation or retardation (Q6 score 3), and recurrent thoughts of death (Q10 score 2). A total ≥14 plus Q10 ≥1 mandates urgent referral. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange same-day urgent appointment with <med>primary care provider</med> or perinatal mental-health specialist
2. Ensure continuous adult support until professional evaluation; avoid being alone with baby if feeling overwhelmed
3. Develop a written safety plan including crisis hotline numbers and local emergency contacts
4. Involve partner or trusted family member in care discussions and infant-care duties to allow rest
5. Discuss short-term medication options (e.g., <med>SSRI</med>) and therapy referrals; do not delay treatment planning
6. Schedule follow-up within 48 hours to reassess mood, safety, and medication adherence
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Post-delivery mother (infant age not specified)  
Date: [today]

Symptoms endorsed (≥ 2 weeks):
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness, anhedonia
- Marked guilt/self-blame regarding infant care
- Generalized & infant-focused anxiety, panic episodes
- Initial insomnia, middle-of-night rumination
- Overwhelming fatigue/“can’t cope”
- Passive self-harm ideation (no plan, no intent)

Pattern: Consistent with moderate–severe postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety.

Red-flag safety item: Passive suicidal thoughts (“what if I weren’t here”) reported twice this week; no preparatory behavior, but distress and fear about the thoughts noted.

Risk factors identified: Primiparity (?), sleep deprivation, absence of perceived enjoyment, intrusive worries re: infant safety, social masking (“told Mom I’m fine”).

Screening impression: High clinical likelihood of major postpartum depressive episode with anxious features; rule-out postpartum anxiety disorder; safety risk present and requires immediate follow-up.

Next step: Recommend same-day safety assessment and formal diagnostic evaluation; consider expedited referral to perinatal mental-health specialty and/or crisis support.
